title: Replace NIP-BE
body:
This PR is a complete rewrite of NIP-BE around the transport dipity runs on iOS and Android. I opted to replace BE instead of add a new NIP, or follow the existing NIP for the following reasons:

- There appears to be only one implementation, samiz.
- In the current NIP, a passive scanner can follow any phone running it, because the advertisement carries a device UUID that the one implementation keeps for the life of the install.
- Anyone in range can read every event, filter and pubkey two phones exchange, because messages travel in plaintext.
- Two iPhones cannot find each other, because roles are assigned by comparing device UUIDs read from service data, and iOS cannot advertise service data.
- Traffic is not encrypted in the current version.
- Authentication is not defined in the current version.
- This version adds an explicit pairing code.
- This version enables a full-duplex client/relay message protocol.
- This version supports syncing media using a modified blossom protocol and incremental sync/validation using blake3 hashes.
- This version adds an optional L2CAP channel for blob traffic, inside the same Noise session, because GATT tops out around 5 to 15 KB/s.

This will be implemented in the next version of https://gitea.coracle.social/coracle/dipity

title: add NIP-402: L402 authentication for paid relays
body:
Bind the L402 protocol (Lightning HTTP 402) to the nostr relay protocol so a relay can charge for access with a self-verifying, payment-bound bearer credential carried in-band over the WebSocket, instead of an out-of-band payment page plus pubkey whitelisting. A relay sends a macaroon and a BOLT 11/BOLT 12 invoice in an L402 challenge; the client pays, obtains the preimage, and presents the macaroon:preimage credential, answered with a dedicated L402-OK message. The relay verifies statelessly by re-deriving the macaroon's root key from a master secret and checking the preimage against the committed payment hash, with no per-credential or per-pubkey database.

Macaroon caveats scope the credential (kinds, operations, authors, tags, validity window, size) and meter usage (event/byte budgets, subscription and rate ceilings, retention); the caveats are the access control, so a relay rejects any condition it does not recognize and mints a distinct invoice per credential. Two new machine-readable prefixes, payment-required: and subscription-limit-reached:, are defined, and the NIP takes the decimal id 402 (the HTTP "Payment Required" status L402 is named for), which also fits NIP-11's integer supported_nips list.

Update README: add the NIP-402 entry and register the L402 and L402-OK messages in the message type tables.

title: NIP-XX: Peer-to-peer Order and Trade events for non-Bitcoin assets
body:
## Summary

This NIP defines addressable events (kind `35353`) for peer-to-peer orders of crypto assets and platform balances **other than bitcoin**, traded against fiat, plus a `trade` document that records each execution.

It is meant for markets where most P2P volume happens in stablecoins and other assets against local currencies, typically in regions with capital controls. These markets have the same liquidity fragmentation that NIP-69 addresses, and they also lack signed reports of executed prices.

## Why not extend NIP-69?

- **`amt` is not compatible.** NIP-69 expresses `amt` in satoshis. Here it is in the asset's main unit, so a NIP-69 client reading an order for `250` USDT would interpret it as `250` sats. Reusing kind `38383` would break existing clients.
- **NIP-69 is already deployed.** It is implemented by several platforms (Mostro, lnp2pBot, Robosats, Peach), and changing its semantics would break them.
- **There is no overlap.** This NIP MUST NOT be used for BTC, L-BTC or RBTC, including custodial bitcoin balances. Bitcoin orders stay on NIP-69, so there is still only one way to publish a bitcoin order.
- **Tag names come from NIP-69 where the meaning is the same** (`k`, `f`, `s`, `amt`, `fa`, `pm`, `y`, `z`, …), so existing implementations can reuse most of their code.

## What it adds

- **Asset identity.** `c` (ticker), `layer`, `network` and `contract` identify an asset. Contract addresses are normalized per chain so that clients can group by them. Platform-internal balances (`layer` = `internal`) also include the platform pubkey, since they are only fungible within that platform.
- **Fixed prices.** An order includes exactly one of `price` or `premium`, because many target markets have no reliable public reference price.
- **Strict number format.** Unsigned decimal strings, with a grammar.
- **Trades.** Every execution of a published order is published as a `trade`, with `executed_at` and the executed `amt` / `fa`. This gives a signed execution history from which anyone can compute market prices, while the signature only proves what the platform states. Multi-fill orders are fully specified.
- **Security and privacy considerations.** These cover what a signature proves, how to avoid linking trades to bank transfers, and how to aggregate correctly.

## Status

- `draft` `optional`. Clients and relays that don't implement it are not affected.
- Kind `35353` is not used by any other NIP.
- The example events are validly signed with a test key.
- Implementations: none listed yet. Feedback on the format is welcome before implementation.

title: NIP-XX: Namecoin resolution for nsites
body:
## Summary

Adds a draft NIP for resolving a Namecoin name to a [NIP-5A](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/5A.md) nsite.

The canonical record field is `nostr.nsite`, containing one NIP-19 pointer:

| Pointer | Selected target |
| --- | --- |
| `npub` or `nprofile` | Current kind `15128` root site |
| `naddr` | Current kind `15128` root site (empty identifier) or current kind `35128` named site (exact identifier) |
| `nevent` or `note` | Exact kind `15128`, `35128`, or `5128` manifest event |

The draft preserves the existing identity-to-root flow and the experimental `nsite: "blog"` named-site shorthand. It also documents the previously deployed simple pubkey, single-identity, and NIP-05-style `names` record forms.

## Resolution and security behavior

- A direct NIP-19 pointer takes exclusive precedence over legacy identity fields.
- `nostr.nsite` is canonical. A top-level `nsite` alias is accepted only for compatibility and never overrides the nested field.
- A malformed or unavailable direct target fails closed. It does not fall back to a legacy identity, an older manifest, DNS, or an ordinary website.
- Bare named-site identifiers still require an unambiguous legacy author.
- Multiple legacy `names` entries without `_` are ambiguous and are not selected by JSON member order.
- Strict NIP-19 TLV lengths and cardinality prevent decoder-specific duplicate-field behavior.
- Replaceable manifests follow NIP-01 ordering after id/signature and coordinate checks, including lowest-id tie breaking. An invalid selected event does not revive an older one.
- Exact event pointers retain their event-id pinning. Exact kind `15128` or `35128` events are never rewritten to current-site or snapshot URLs.
- `.bit` resolution walks `map` from the registered base name; ifa-0001 imports have deterministic precedence and fail closed when they affect the selected target.
- The trust model distinguishes blockchain-verified resolution from explicitly trusted ElectrumX/indexer services. TLS or server agreement alone is not called blockchain authentication.
- Snapshots remain immutable and are not presented as current live sites.
- Signature, manifest, path-hash, Blossom retrieval, and per-blob SHA-256 verification are required by this naming profile.

This is a naming specification only. It does not define DNS, HTTPS interception, TLSA, or ordinary-web transport.

## Compatibility example

A publisher can retain a NIP-05 identity while pointing the name at an independent named site:

```json
{
  "nostr": {
    "nsite": "naddr1...",
    "names": {
      "_": "<identity-pubkey>"
    }
  }
}
```

The identity remains available to Namecoin NIP-05 clients. nsite resolvers use the explicit `naddr` target.

Older records continue to support:

```json
{ "nostr": "<root-author-hex-pubkey>" }
```

and the experimental named-site shorthand:

```json
{
  "nostr": {
    "pubkey": "<author-hex-pubkey>",
    "nsite": "blog"
  }
}
```

## Related proposals

- Owned Namecoin-track draft: [mstrofnone/nips#2](https://github.com/mstrofnone/nips/pull/2); ngit proposal: [`74c8668e…`](https://gitworkshop.dev/npub1gvv9ahktvavf9qjtrgm62le7gplmmchd5usp5wpfhr85hf79kncqj8xchs/wss%3A%2F%2Frelay.ngit.dev/nips/pulls/74c8668e5fc912aa3f09b2e096f3d124e3ab786e5ed51cac3c5243438177cf15).
- [#2349](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2349) defines the Namecoin `nostr` container and NIP-05 identity lookup behavior used by this draft.
- [#2353](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2353) defines `namecoin:name:<namespace>/<name>` for optional NIP-73 discovery metadata. The new draft requires reverse Namecoin resolution before treating a manifest's self-declared alias as verified.
- [NIP-5A](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/5A.md) remains authoritative for manifests, canonical gateway URLs, snapshots, paths, and Blossom content.

## Implementation work

[hzrd149/nsite-gateway#24](https://github.com/hzrd149/nsite-gateway/pull/24) is the reference implementation surface for the legacy forms and direct-pointer resolution.

The specification's JSON examples were parsed programmatically. Its `nprofile`, named `naddr`, and root `naddr` examples were also decoded with `nostr-tools`; the root coordinate has kind `15128` and an empty identifier. This validation does not imply that existing NIP-5A clients automatically understand Namecoin or the new `nsite` field.

title: Add logout to nip 47
body:
NWC connection URLs are useful not only to connect clients, but also to implement subscriptions. In the case of a leak though, it's very bad for a service provider to be unable to prevent an attacker from draining users' wallets. `logout` is good hygiene for when a user logs out of an application, but also provides a way to mitigate harm when connection URLs are leaked.

Please tag wallet providers.

title: NIP-XX: Agent Coordination and Off-Relay Listing Reviews
body:
Opening this as a draft to get feedback before it's ready for review. I know there's one implementation so far, and the README asks for two clients.

## What it adds

Two regular kinds:

- **`4200` Coordination message.** JSON `act` vocabulary (Contract-Net announce/bid/award plus propose/accept/reject/inform) on `t`-tagged subchats, threaded with NIP-10.
- **`4201` Listing review.** `{rating: -1|0|1, comment?}` about a listing that lives **off Nostr**, referenced with a NIP-73 external id: `["i", "arweave:tx:<txid>"]`, `["k", "arweave:tx"]`.

No listing kind is defined. The listings are signed JSON on a permanent content-addressed store (Arweave in the reference implementation), because the registry must not be editable or deletable and shouldn't depend on any relay's retention policy. Nostr carries only the cheap parts: negotiation and reviews.

## Questions I'd like feedback on

1. **Should reviews be a NIP-32 label instead of a new kind?** The draft argues for a dedicated kind (fixed machine-checked shape, a plain `kinds` filter), but it's written so it could become an `L`/`l` namespace while keeping the same `i`/`k` reference.
2. **Is `arweave:tx:<txid>` an acceptable NIP-73 id?** Arweave ids are base64url, so they're case-sensitive, unlike the hex chains in NIP-73's examples.
3. **Overlap with the open agent PRs** (#2445, #2221, #2226, #2246, #1929). The draft's niche is a registry kept off relays, and `4201` can review listings announced by any of them. Happy to align if one of those is converging.

## Running implementation

- Client, MCP server and specs (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Technosophorso/oracle
- Relay carrying both kinds: `wss://relay.parles.xyz` (strfry, with the NIP-11 extension described in the draft)
- Domain bootstrap file: https://parles.xyz/.well-known/agent-marketplace.json
- Example listing: Arweave tx `0NAb46_EcAlMZ11rMggjgmd6FsSPKkSBbrOvKbrqubg`

The prose in NIP-F4 calls the authored-podcasts list `kind:10164`, but the example event right below it, the NIP-51 standard lists table, and the README event kinds table all use `10064`. This changes the one sentence to match.

title: NIP-XX: Repost attribution (via tag)
body:
When someone likes or replies to a note they saw through Alice's repost, Alice never finds out. This lets the client add Alice as a `p` tag, plus a `via` tag that explains why she's tagged:

```
["via", "<repost-event-id>", "<relay-url>", "<reposter-pubkey>"]
```

Clients that don't support this show a plain mention.

Prior art: Bluesky's `via` on likes and reposts (bluesky-social/atproto#3882). Related: #367.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: NIP-F8: Visit Counter
body:
Defines how clients report visits to addressable content and how a relay publishes hourly visit statistics for it.

- `kind:20918` (ephemeral): a visit, with a single `a` tag pointing to the visited content.
- The relay deduplicates visits per clock hour (UTC) by pubkey and by source IP, and does not count the author's own visits.
- `kind:30918` (addressable): daily (hourly breakdown) and all-time statistics, signed by the relay key advertised in the NIP-11 `self` field.
- Statistics are private to the author: the relay only delivers them to a NIP-42 connection authenticated as the pubkey in the `p` tag.
- Optional `GET /visit?a=...` pixel endpoint for clients that only load images.

Implementation in nostr-rs-relay (SQLite): https://github.com/robersonfox/nostr-rs-relay/tree/feat/visit-counter

title: NIP-D9: Deletion Request Protection
body:
## Problem

Nostr deletion requests assume the key signing an event can retract it later. Applications that share signing keys or retain protocol history cannot use that authority safely: any key holder can request removal of events that other participants still need.

## Fix

Propose a signed `no_delete` marker that exempts an event from deletion requests through its own signing key, with explicit NIP-09 and NIP-62 exceptions. Preserve recipient and delegator deletion authority, the event's original expiration, and independent relay policy. Expiration does not end the marker's protection, including for expired copies a relay retains.

## Status

NIP-D9 is the proposed designation, pending acceptance. This is a protocol proposal with required-behavior scenarios; no client or relay implementation is included.

## Validation

Checked local Markdown links, JSON examples, and whitespace. The scenarios cover deletion-before-event ordering, republication, mixed targets, expiration, recipient and delegator authority, and malformed tags.

title: remove the embed from the c7 reply example
README: register kinds 3711, 3712, 9042-9044 and 9061 (NKIPs)
body:
These kinds are used by three open, CC0 specs at nkips.org (No-KYC Improvement Proposals). We're registering them so they don't collide with future assignments.

- **3711 / 3712** ([NKIP-0001](https://nkips.org/nkip-0001/)): a swap exchange signs a hash of each order's deposit and payout addresses before showing the deposit address (3711). Hourly Merkle roots timestamp those hashes (3712), so users can later prove what they were promised. No plaintext addresses or amounts go on relays.
- **9042 / 9043 / 9044** ([NKIP-0002](https://nkips.org/nkip-0002/)): a Monero tip receipt (9042), a payment proof sent only to the recipient as an unsigned NIP-59 rumor inside a gift wrap (9043), and the recipient's public confirmation (9044). Clients can show verified tips without any txid becoming public. 9042 is already published by Ripley Terminal.
- **9061** ([NKIP-0006](https://nkips.org/nkip-0006/)): a PGP-encrypted, PGP-signed chat message between people whose identity is a PGP key, published from a fresh key each time and found by a single-letter `z` tag that changes daily.

All are regular events, optional for clients and relays; nothing stops working for software that ignores them. Specs, JSON schemas and test vectors: https://github.com/nkips/nkips

Disclosure: the NKIPs are written by the authors of kyc.rip, xmr.club and Ripley Terminal, which are the current implementations.

title: NIP-XX: Cashtags ($TICKER mentions with an optional asset id)
body:
Notes already use `$XMR`, `$BTC` and so on, and clients turn them into price
chips, but every client tokenizes and guesses the asset differently. This NIP
defines how `$TICKER` is found in text and adds one optional `cashtag` tag,
so the author can name the exact asset (CAIP-19 or a short id) and choose a
compact chip or an expanded card. Clients that ignore the tag still see plain
text. Search uses ordinary `t` tags (`$xmr`), so relays need no changes.

Implemented by Ripley Terminal (writer and reader). Test vectors (tokenizer,
events, search, display) and a stdlib checker:
https://github.com/nkips/nkips/tree/main/nkips/nkip-0005 . Looking for a
second client to implement it before this leaves draft.

Disclosure: written by the Ripley Terminal authors; the longer version lives
at https://nkips.org/nkip-0005/ and will point here once merged.

title: NIP-XX: DNS delegation for NIP-05 (discussion)
body:
This proposal is submitted for discussion and design feedback before implementation.

An organization may use different providers for its website and Nostr identifiers. This draft lets it publish a TXT record at `_nip05.<domain>` naming a NIP-05 provider. Public keys and relay metadata remain in the existing HTTPS JSON response; the delegated request adds a `domain` parameter for providers serving multiple domains.

Ordinary NIP-05 takes precedence. Clients query DNS only after the original HTTPS endpoint returns **404 Not Found or 410 Gone**. Timeouts, TLS errors, redirects, other HTTP errors, malformed JSON, missing names, and key mismatches do not trigger delegation. Once DNS discovery starts, absent or invalid delegation and lookup failures fail the request; clients do not return to the original endpoint.

Successful ordinary lookups require no additional DNS/DoH query. Browser clients can use DoH for the fallback, but must be able to read the original 404/410 through CORS. A blocked or opaque response is not an absence signal. Older clients cannot resolve identifiers served only through delegation.

DNSSEC remains recommended rather than mandatory. With unsigned DNS, a valid TLS certificate for the selected provider does not prove authorization by the original domain. DoH protects the resolver connection but does not itself establish DNSSEC validation.

Feedback is welcome on whether this is useful as a separate extension, the 404/410 trigger, and the tradeoffs of optional DNSSEC. The precedence and shorter motivation reflect the review discussion on this PR.

Related discussions: #29 (SRV delegation), #146 (identities in TXT records), and #2516 (organizational delegation). Redirects remain prohibited under NIP-05; #1544 discusses that alternative.

This submission contains the specification only; no implementation or interoperability results are included. The identifier is `XX` pending discussion.

title: NIP-A3: add the `bip321` payto type
body:
Hi, I'm Matthew from Second, the team behind Bark, an Ark implementation.

This adds `bip321` to the commonly used `payto` types, plus a short section on how to use it:

```json
["payto", "bip321", "bitcoin:?ark=ark1p...&lno=lno1..."]
```

The value is a full BIP-321 URI. One entry can offer several static ways to pay the same person (an on-chain address, `sp=`, a BOLT12 offer, an Ark address), and the payer's wallet picks the one it can use. The rules are deliberately small:

- static, reusable instructions only: no BOLT11 invoice and no `amount`, since the entry is paid many times by different people;
- the payer chooses the amount, and a client with Nostr Wallet Connect hands the URI to NWC-321 `pay`, so the wallet, not the client, picks the rail;
- `bip353` names resolve to the same kind of URI, and a `lightning` entry stays useful as a fallback.

Why a URI instead of one more type per rail: BIP-321 already is the container for "several ways to pay one person", and wallets already parse it. A separate `ark` type (or a type per new rail) would make every client learn each rail, while a `bip321` entry passes straight through to the wallet. It also avoids a new kind for profile payment targets.

We use this entry in a rework of #2521 (zaps over BIP-321 rails), where `kind:10133` with a `bip321` entry becomes the recipient's zap target. This PR stands on its own, though: any client can show the entry as a "pay" button today.

This is a draft, and we're still working out the smoothest payment experience across Nostr, so feedback on the rules above (or the name) is very welcome.

title: NIP-XX: Zaps over BIP-321 rails
body:
Hi, I'm Matthew from Second, the team behind Bark, an Ark implementation.

This draft defines zaps that can be paid over any rail a recipient offers in a BIP-321 URI: Ark, Lightning or on-chain, next to NIP-57 and NIP-61. It started as Ark-only zaps; this version generalises it so the zap layer doesn't care which rail settled the payment. It is a draft and open to revision: we're still working out the smoothest payment experience and would like your feedback.

**The principle.** Payments between two users of the same Ark server should settle natively over Ark: self-custodial VTXOs with a unilateral exit, instant, near-free, and the recipient can be offline. Between different Ark servers, and with everyone else, Lightning. And it should build on what already exists rather than add parallel formats: BIP-321 for the request, NWC-321 `pay` for the wallet call, NIP-A3 for the profile entry, NIP-57 for the receipt model.

**How it works**

- **Recipient:** a `bip321` payto entry in `kind:10133` (NIP-A3; small PR: https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/pull/2522), e.g. `bitcoin:?ark=<ark address>&lno=<bolt12 offer>`, plus a `receipt-key` tag in the same event. The tag is the opt-in, and names the key that signs receipts (the user's own key, or one held by a wallet service).
- **Sender:** pays the URI with NWC-321 `pay` and an amount. The wallet picks the rail: an `ark=` on its own Ark server, else Lightning (`lno=`), else on-chain. The client never chooses. It then publishes `kind:9740` with the usual `p`/`e`/`a`/`k` targets, `amount` in msats, the `rail`, and a NIP-44 encrypted payment reference (Ark: VTXO outpoints + address; Lightning: payment hash; on-chain: txid).
- **Receipt:** one kind for every rail, `kind:9741`, signed by the receipt key after it finds the payment in the wallet. It copies the target tags, so clients count `9741` and `9735` together with one `#e` filter.
- Recipients with only a Lightning address keep getting NIP-57 zaps; Ark wallets pay those through their server's Lightning gateway.

**Trust model.** None of these rails can be checked by third parties from public data, so, like NIP-57, the receipt comes from the recipient's side, signed by a key the recipient chose rather than a separate LNURL provider. An unconfirmed `kind:9740` is never counted, and the encrypted reference can't be copied into someone else's zap, so senders can't inflate totals. References stay private (no VTXO ids, payment hashes or txids in the clear); the spec notes the remaining on-chain linking risk.

Compared with v1: `kind:10740` is gone (the payment target is NIP-A3's `kind:10133`), the receipt is rail-neutral, and `ark-server`/`ark-payment` became `rail`/`payment`. Kind numbers are still placeholders.

Related drafts that use the same BIP-321 + NWC-321 model:

- NWC Ark Payments, https://github.com/nostr-wallet-connect/nwc/pull/11 (the `ark` instruction and payment details)
- Blossom BUD-07 `X-Ark`, https://github.com/hzrd149/blossom/pull/116 (paid uploads with a BIP-321 request)

Views welcome especially on two points: whether `receipt-key` belongs in `kind:10133` (we chose it so one event says both "how to pay me" and "who confirms", and rotating one updates both), and whether one receipt kind for every rail is the right shape.

title: NIP-47: make the core wording payment-rail neutral
body:
NIP-47 describes "a lightning wallet". Since #2419, new wallet features live in [NWC extension specs](https://github.com/nostr-wallet-connect/nwc), and some of those now define payment rails other than Lightning. The first is Ark, proposed in https://github.com/nostr-wallet-connect/nwc/pull/11, which Bark, Arkade and Wavelength wallets would serve.

This PR only adjusts the core wording so it doesn't assume Lightning is the only rail:

- The wallet is "a bitcoin wallet". The core commands use Lightning, and extensions may add other rails.
- Extensions that define a rail may add their own commands, `get_info` fields and notification payloads. Clients SHOULD ignore `get_info` fields they don't recognize.
- `balance` and `network` cover every rail the wallet supports.

No command, field or behaviour changes. Existing wallets and clients are unaffected.

Opened as a draft alongside the extension PR.

title: Passkey-held Nostr keys and optional vaults
body:
This proposal defines passkey-held Nostr keys with an explicit distinction between derived keys and encrypted existing keys, so clients recover the intended identity. It specifies a shared recovery format and an optional companion for seed and multi-account vaults.

Related work: Passkey-Wrapped Keys / Nosskey (#1919) previously proposed both approaches but was closed without merging. This proposal revisits that work with explicit key-mode identification and interoperable recovery records.

NIP numbers and relay kind 31778 remain provisional.

title: NIP-01: define subscription replacement and refused-REQ behaviour
body:
NIP-01 says a `REQ` that reuses a subscription id creates a new subscription "replacing the old one", but it never defines what replacing means. Relays differ in practice, so clients that change filters often (for example, rotating an `authors` list) can't rely on in-place replacement today.

Measured against five relays (local, default configs, October 2026), plus nostrfy as reported by its maintainer in this thread:

| Relay | Behaviour when a `REQ` reuses an active subscription id |
|---|---|
| strfry 1.1.3 | Replaces, but drops events accepted in the ~100 ms before the swap that the old filters matched, including events the new filters also match. Live fan-out is debounced, and the old monitor is removed before it processes the pending batch. |
| khatru v0.19.1 | Doesn't replace. Adds the new filters next to the old ones, so events matching only the old filters keep arriving and overlapping events arrive twice, until the client sends `CLOSE`. (Fixed in current fiatjaf.com/nostr khatru.) |
| khatru (current, fiatjaf.com/nostr) | Removes the old filters, runs the new initial query, then installs the new filters. Events arriving during that query are lost. |
| nostr-rs-relay 0.10.0 | Replaces atomically. |
| wok 0.7.0 | Replaces atomically. |
| nostrfy 0.1.23 | Replaces the filters (never merges them), but discards the old subscription's queued initial-query events and buffered live events on the swap. Live batches received before the `REQ` but processed after it are matched against the new filters, so events that matched only the old filters can be lost. |

Separately, strfry and wok answer a refused replacement (filter too large, rate-limited) with `CLOSED` for the id but keep delivering events on the old filters under that id. That contradicts `CLOSED`'s definition ("a subscription was ended on the server side"). nostrfy already ends the old subscription in that case.

## Change

- New paragraph after "Upon receiving a `REQ` message…" defining replacement, stated in terms of what the client receives:
  - The new filters replace the old ones entirely and are never merged with them.
  - Once the relay receives the new `REQ`, it may stop serving the old filters straight away, including abandoning their unfinished initial query. It must not send an `EOSE` for the old filters, so the client doesn't get two.
  - Any events the relay still sends because of the old filters come before the `EOSE`/`CLOSED` that answers the new `REQ`.
  - The swap must not lose a newly received event that matches the new filters: neither one the old filters also matched that hadn't been sent yet, nor one that arrives while the new initial query runs.
  - The new initial query may repeat events, so clients should deduplicate by id.
- `CLOSED` bullet: a refused `REQ` gets no `EOSE`. If the refused `REQ` reused an active id, the `CLOSED` also ends the previous subscription, and no further events are sent under that id until a new `REQ` is accepted. Adds two refusal examples (`rate-limited:`, `invalid:`).

Nothing else changes: no new message types, prefixes or NIP-11 fields.

## Notes

- **Revised after review.** The first version required relays to deliver everything the old filters had matched before the swap, which also forced them to finish an unfinished old initial query. That described relay internals and ruled out abandoning a stale query. Events that match only the old filters may now be dropped at the swap. The no-loss rule covers only events the new filters match.
- **One race remains.** An `EOSE` the relay sent for the old filters before it received the new `REQ` can still reach the client afterwards. Fixing that needs a new message type, which is out of scope.
- **Out of scope.** NIP-01 already requires `EOSE` after the initial queries when `limit` is `0`, and `CLOSED` when a relay refuses a `REQ`. Some relays violate both rules today. Those are separate implementation bugs, and this PR doesn't touch either rule.
- **Refused replacement ends the old subscription instead of keeping it.** `CLOSED` already means the subscription was ended, and keeping the old filters alive would make `CLOSED` ambiguous.

title: NIP-40: clarify that an event is expired at its expiration timestamp
body:
Clarify that an event is expired once the current time reaches its `expiration` value, so `now == expiration` already counts as expired. NIP-40 currently says the timestamp is the point "at which the message SHOULD be considered expired" but does not say which side of that second the boundary falls on.

Most implementations already agree. strfry, nostr-rs-relay, nostream, khatru, mattn/nostr-relay and cagliostr all treat `expiration <= now` as expired. rnostr is the exception and uses `expiration < now`, keeping the event valid for one more second.

I also published test events to 10 public relays that advertise NIP-40 (strfry from 0.9.6 to 1.1.3, and nostr-rs-relay 0.9.0). All of them rejected an event whose `expiration` equaled the current second as expired and accepted one expiring a second later.

title: NIP-62: clarify re-admission after a vanish request
body:
NIP-62 requires paid relays and relays that restrict who can post to honor a request to vanish regardless of the user's status, but it does not say whether a vanished pubkey may later be re-admitted as a member. Relays otherwise diverge, and a relay that excludes a pubkey permanently can still diverge between live state and state rebuilt from stored events.

This PR states that re-admission is relay policy, and that a relay which keeps a vanished pubkey permanently excluded MUST apply the same policy when membership state is rebuilt.

No wire-format change.

Implementation context: iqbqioza/nostrfy#241 validates NIP-43 joins for freshness and vanished keys.

title: NIP-59: refuse re-storing deleted gift wraps
body:
NIP-59 tells relays to delete `kind:1059` events that p-tag the signer of a NIP-09 deletion or a NIP-62 vanish request, but nothing prevents the same wrap from being stored again when it is re-broadcast, silently undoing the recipient's deletion. NIP-62 already requires that deleted events cannot be re-broadcasted; the same guarantee is needed for gift wraps deleted under NIP-59.

This PR adds one sentence requiring relays to refuse re-storing a `kind:1059` event whose id they deleted under this rule.

No wire-format change.

Implementation context: iqbqioza/nostrfy#242 blocks a re-broadcast of a recipient-deleted gift wrap.

title: NIP-XX: Interactive Charts (kind 1786)
body:
This proposes `kind:1786`, a regular event whose `.content` is a declarative chart. Notes could then embed interactive charts (tooltips, hover highlighting, zoom) instead of screenshots or links to chart sites.

**How it works**

- **Content.** The content is JSON in a versioned dialect named by a tag: `["dialect", "vega-lite-nostr", "1"]`. Version 1 is a closed subset of Vega-Lite with no expressions, transforms, URLs or renderer config. Every valid document is also a valid Vega-Lite spec. Web clients can render it with Vega-Lite, and native clients can map its seven mark types onto their own chart toolkits.
- **Embedding.** Notes, comments and articles embed a chart the way they quote any other event: a `nostr:nevent1…` reference plus a `q` tag. A required `alt` tag gives screen readers, and clients that don't support charts, a text description.
- **Regular kind, not addressable.** Replies, reactions and zaps stay bound to the exact data. A correction is a new event that points back to the old chart with a `supersedes` role.
- **Rendering rules.** Clients validate charts against an allow-list. They never run author code and make no network requests for a chart. Web clients render each chart in a sandboxed iframe with a strict CSP.

Several of these rules came out of testing:
- In Vega-Lite 5, a quote in an axis format string runs expression code chosen by the author.
- vega-tooltip's default handler fetches whatever is in a field named `image`.
- Fuzzing found four Vega-Lite compiler crashes that valid-looking specs can trigger. The dialect now excludes them.

**Supporting material**

https://github.com/defauxking/Interactive-Charts-kind-1786 has:
- the JSON Schema the NIP references
- a reference validator with accept/reject test cases
- the example events

The examples in the NIP are real signed events, made with a throwaway key.

**Status and open questions**

No client implements this yet. I'm opening the PR now to get feedback before implementation work starts. I'd especially like opinions on these:

1. Is a Vega-Lite subset the right base, or would a smaller purpose-built grammar be preferred?
2. The draft is long because it defines the dialect inline. Should the dialect move to a separate document?
3. Is kind 1786 acceptable? And is index 3 the right place for the role on `e` tags? NIP-10 and NIP-54 put their markers there.

title: Make NIP-EE a concise reference to Marmot
body:
Replace the obsolete NIP-EE protocol text with a short reference to the adopted Marmot specification, so readers can find the current MLS messaging rules without relying on a second, diverging specification.

The reference explains account identities, MLS key rotation, the three relay roles, and the KeyPackage, Welcome and group event envelopes. Its security section distinguishes receiver account-key compromise from access to MLS secrets and explains which sender and relay information an unwrapped Welcome reveals.

The index restores NIP-EE as the Marmot reference and registers addressable KeyPackages at kind `30443`. Historical kinds `443` and `10051` remain listed as legacy to preserve their allocation history.

## Verification

Compared the event and relay summary against the [adopted Nostr transport](https://github.com/marmot-protocol/marmot/blob/7fabb81b3ed6e2fffeb1b267a0d2ae92b0ab2c89/transports/nostr.md), [NIP-59](https://github.com/nostr-protocol/nips/blob/master/59.md), and [MLS Welcome processing](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9420.html#section-12.4.3). This is a documentation change, not a claim that every Marmot implementation supports the same specification revision.

## Scope

The full Marmot specification remains normative. This change introduces no new event format or client implementation, and does not make older MLS clients interoperable with the current binding.

title: Solve #2482
body:
Solves #2482.

Being able to trivially verify whether a badge has been accepted by a user or not is a desirable feature (for example, when compiling a list of users that have accepted the badge).

I fixed the ambiguities I referenced earlier so as to allow for this without any need for fetching event sets.
